title: Investigators Probe Possible Intoxication in NYC Subway Deaths of Indian-Origin Woman, Friend
excerpt: Malaika Chitre, 24, and Navam Kaul, 24, were struck by a No. 4 train at Lower Manhattan's Spring Street station early Sunday; law-enforcement sources say detectives are examining whether alcohol or drugs left the pair unaware of the danger.
body:
• Law-enforcement sources told the New York Post that detectives are examining whether alcohol or another form of intoxication impaired the judgment of Malaika Chitre, 24, and Navam Kaul, 24, before a subway train killed them — a claim attributed only to those sources, not an established fact.
  • Chitre and Kaul were struck by a southbound No. 4 train at the Spring Street station in Lower Manhattan at about 3:15 a.m. on Sunday, September 13, and were pronounced dead at the scene; about 100 passengers were evacuated from the train.
  • Bystander video appears to show the two sitting on the tracks before the train approached. The operator told supervisors she spotted them and could not stop in time, and reportedly said Chitre appeared to be laughing as she tried to pull Kaul toward her.
  • No suicide note was recovered, no motive has been established, and investigators have not ruled out any possibility, including suicide. Chitre's family has criticized sensational media speculation about the deaths.

The new claim

Two days after the deaths of Malaika Chitre and Navam Kaul, investigators are testing a new line of inquiry: whether one or both were intoxicated when they ended up on the tracks of a Lower Manhattan subway station, law-enforcement sources told the New York Post. Detectives are looking at whether alcohol or drugs dulled their awareness of the danger before a southbound No. 4 train struck them at around 3:15 a.m. on Sunday, September 13. The intoxication theory comes only from those unnamed sources and has not been confirmed by the NYPD or the transit authority.

What happened at Spring Street

Chitre, 24, and Kaul, 24, were hit by a No. 4 train at the Spring Street station and pronounced dead at the scene, police said. Officers were alerted at about 3:14 a.m. after the train was unable to stop; roughly 100 passengers were evacuated onto the platform. The operator told supervisors she spotted the pair on the tracks but could not brake in time. Sources quoted by the Post said Kaul may have fallen or entered the tracks first, prompting Chitre to go down after him; a bystander's video appeared to show the two sitting on the roadbed before the train approached. No suicide note was recovered, and investigators have not ruled out any possibility, including suicide.

Context & background

Chitre and Kaul grew up in nearby towns in New Jersey — Chitre in Dayton, Kaul in Sayreville — and both graduated from Rutgers University in 2024. Kaul's family immigrated from Nepal, and the two belonged to the same South Asian friend circle. "They grew up in the same world," Rajnikant Pipalia, who told the Post his son was a friend of Kaul, said of the group. Chitre, an operations specialist at Acadia Pharmaceuticals, was also pursuing a doctorate in pharmacy at Temple University; Kaul, a business graduate, worked as a financial data analyst at Bloomberg. "We are saddened to learn of the tragic death of these two former students," said Dory Devlin, Rutgers' assistant vice president of news and media relations.

"She used to play with the kids on the block — a bright, smart girl. I was shocked when I heard about this... It's just so weird. I'm still not understanding: why on the track?"

— Neighbour of the Chitre family, quoted in the New York Post

Impact & analysis

The intoxication claim, if confirmed by toxicology results, would answer the question every account keeps returning to: why two young people with no apparent reason to be there were sitting on the tracks at 3:15 in the morning. But it remains a hypothesis relayed by unnamed sources. What is confirmed is thin — the time, the station, the evacuation, the absence of a note — and Chitre's family has publicly criticized media coverage, saying some reports aired sensational speculation without factual basis. Until detectives release findings, the central facts are the operator's account and the video, both showing a pair that seemed unaware of the train bearing down on them.

Diaspora angle

The deaths have hit New Jersey's South Asian community hard; both families are rooted in its diaspora circles, and the story is being followed closely by Indian and Nepali-American outlets in the US and India. For families here, the case is a painful reminder of how quickly grief is compounded when speculation outruns confirmed facts.

What's next

Toxicology results will decide the intoxication theory, and NYPD detectives continue to investigate with no determination yet on how the pair came to be on the tracks. Police said every possibility remains on the table.
image_caption: A figure sits on a New York City subway platform as a train waits beyond the tracks. Investigators are examining whether intoxication played a role in the September 13 deaths of Malaika Chitre and Navam Kaul at the Spring Street No. 4 station.
nri_angle: Two young people rooted in New Jersey's South Asian community died in a tragedy now being picked apart in the press, making careful, attributed reporting — not speculation — the standard their families and community deserve.
author: Diaspora Desk
